prompt: Human: What is a dental implant?
response:
A dental implant is a surgical device that replaces the last molar (or "backothole" in dental terminology) tooth.  It is placed into the jawbone to create a secure anchor for a tooth prosthesis to rest upon when the natural tooth is removed.  Dental implants can restore 100% of your bite, and are very long-lasting.  The implant itself is secured with a titanium post which is integrated with the jawbone.  The post serves to maintain a stable and secure anchor for all types of tooth prosthesis, restoring your smile to the fullness of the natural smile. 
Dental implants are an excellent alternative to the traditional removable partial denture, which can lose its support after some time. 

In North America, about 19% of the population has dental implants.  In China, the number of people who have implants is still relatively low, at about 1% of the population.  This, while quite impressive for a rapidly developing country, does not represent the magnitude of the potential market for dental implants.  It is hypothesized that China has some of the highest rates of gum disease in the world, which could directly account for this paucity of implants.  Even so, China does produce one of the best-known dental implant brands in the world, the Biolase brand (see links below on how to purchase). 
In South Korea, over 80% of the population have dental implants. 
In Sweden the number of patients who have dental implants is approximately 25%, while in the Netherlands it is more than 30%, and Australia is over 40%. 
This last number is a bit misleading, since the patients are probably split into two groups: patients who have not already lost all their teeth due to periodontal disease or decay, and individuals who have lost all their natural teeth and have replaced them with implants.  
There are many studies showing the benefits of implants, including those that compare dental implant patients to those who only receive oral hygiene habits.  
A large study done in France found dental implants to have an average life of about 15 years, compared with seven years for retained teeth. This study concluded that implants were worth the cost. 
To increase the success rate and longevity of implants, dentists use bone grafting to stimulate the jawbone in the days following surgery.  Once the jawbone has reabsorbed the graft it is safe to plan and perform implants. 

Most often implants are made of titanium.  The titanium becomes used to the jawbone, creating a bond between the implant and the jawbone, helping to maintain the stability of the implant and the stability of the jawbone.  Titanium is also known for it's excellent corrosion resistance, and it rarely breaks down over time.  
To ensure that the implant matches the existing colour of the jawbone, a tiny powder is mixed with distilled water to form a paste and mixed with the implant, creating an inert paste which helps retain the implant in the jawbone.  
The most severe complication from implant surgery is infection.  The implant site is therefore meticulously cleaned and sterilized with non-toxic cleaner for days after the implant procedure, and the patient usually receives antibiotics before and after surgery.

prompt: Human: How do I get over guilt?
response:
That's a complex issue.  Guilt can be a healthy emotion, but if you feel that you are carrying that emotion inside you all the time, that can be a problem.  It's possible that your emotions are signals from your mind that something is wrong with you, and it's this emotional feedback that makes you feel guilty.  If that's the case, then an experiment you could try is this:  Take a sheet of paper and write down a specific, identifiable wrong thing that you have done.  For instance, you could write "I ate junk food".  But it has to be a thing you DID, not something you might have done.  Then when you feel that emotion of guilty guilt, write down that emotion on the sheet of paper next to your heart.  I guarantee that when you write that guilt emotion, it will probably go away within a minute.  If it doesn't, then take a short break and come back to it, and repeat the process.

How does that work?  Well if you are feeling guilty, then you probably have some feelings of inadequacy at the very least.  But what I really expect will happen is that you'll start noticing when you are feeling those inner feelings, and then for those few minutes, you won't feel guilty.  You're aware of the emotion, but you aren't attached to it.  
As for what else to do -- that depends a lot on what exactly it is that you feel guilty about.  But one approach might be to just accept and tolerate the experience.  In some ways I suspect you will feel better once you accept that this feeling of guilty guilt actually does have a legitimate basis in reality.  The fact that it is a real feeling won't change much.  If you do accept it for what it is and let it pass by you in a short time, you will likely feel better.  Acceptance of emotions that are real, as well as emotions that are not real, is one key step in dealing with pain.  For instance, you might accept your guilt, then experience the emotion of anger, and then start a new conversation, or learn to be kinder to yourself, even though you feel guilty.  
Perhaps you feel guilty because you are worried that you are a bad parent, so that's a good target to work in a more concrete way.  If so, it might be helpful to look at how your worries about parenting might have come about.  Are you worried that you are a poor parent?  That you're unprepared for the job?  Are you worried you are failing someone who is really important to you?  You could use these kinds of questions to work out what makes you feel worried, then go into a conversation where you really put your concerns on the table and have an honest exchange of emotions and ideas, with yourself and the other person.

But actually, the opposite is true: since organic food was introduced in the 1980s, nutrition quality metrics for various food groups have been comparable to those of non-organic foods. For example, vitamin C, folate and magnesium in particular are higher in organic foods.  

So, does this mean eating organic food is good?

In a word, yes. Eating organic food might provide some additional health benefits, but the evidence for its increased nutritional quality and/or increased safety is fairly weak.

For instance, we know that organic food contains higher concentrations of vitamins A and C, iron and zinc, but evidence that organic food actually causes these nutrients to be absorbed more easily, or have better bioavailability is weak. Some studies do indicate organic food contains fewer pesticides residues. But pesticides are a global issue, and evidence shows that the U.S. is much worse at controlling them than some other countries.  

Regarding health problems, the studies that are available are mixed. One theory is that eating organic food can provide health benefits against certain cancers. But there’s not much evidence that organic food is more nutritious, and recent studies show that organic food contains slightly higher levels of several types of nutrients, including blood minerals, vitamin E, magnesium, zinc, iron and vitamin A. So organic food shouldn’t be used to claim an extra health benefit from eating it.  

We know that organic food contains higher levels of certain nutrients than non-organic food, including selenium, iron, vitamin A and certain minerals such as manganese, copper, zinc and sodium.

 

But these differences are probably due to biological variation in the foods and populations that consume them. There’s lots of conflicting information out there about the effects of organic food on health, including some study that reported lower levels of cancer, which the author concluded must be the result of differences in genetics and/or diet. (And perhaps most misleadingly, the study reported these lower cancer rates with the organic products.)

 

In case you’re wondering, yes, you can eat organic food every day and not get all the health benefits from it. prompt: Human: Wearing cotton makes me curious, how is it harvested?
response:
That's a great question, and there are several ways.  One common way is through mechanical means, where a machine is used to strip the leaves off the cotton stalks.  There is also a form of manual picking, where one person picks the cotton leaf from a stem while another person holds the stalk and removes the leaves.  A somewhat more environmentally friendly way of harvesting cotton involves a machine that uses water to wash the cotton and break it down into its component fibers.  Once it is stripped of its original fibers, it is typically ground down into a fine powder, which is then turned into a fabric.  A third way of processing cotton involves the use of chemicals like sulfite, which will weaken the fibers.  With all of these methods of processing, there is always a risk of chemicals leaching into the water or air.  Additionally, over-processing can result in damage to beneficial microorganisms that have adapted to thrive in the soil.  Another benefit to mechanical or manual harvesting is the removal of weeds, and these will grow back after cotton has been replaced with new cotton plants.  To fully understand how cotton is harvested, one must also understand that it is grown across three different regions: India, Brazil, and the United States.  

It is important to understand the environmental impact that can result from cotton farming.  For example, it uses about thirty percent of all the water in the United States and about four percent of all the natural gas, which results in high air pollution levels.  In addition, there are human impacts associated with cotton farming.  The industry employs fifty-two million people worldwide, with about two-thirds of those jobs coming from the United States, Brazil, and India.  These jobs are scattered throughout the rural areas, which adds to a greater level of poverty, particularly in developing countries, and a sense of community isolation.  

Cotton farming is also associated with a high level of social inequality.  While the top one percent of American cotton farmers make about $88 million each and the bottom ten percent have incomes of less than a dollar, the overall rate of income equality is only around one-third of that.   While income from cotton farming is relatively low, it still provides a livelihood and access to credit for many of the people, as they are often the last source of income for families.  

If you want to learn more about cotton farming and its impact on people, the environment, and society, there is an organization called the Textile Exchange that publishes research about sustainable cotton practices.  They advocate policies to make cotton farming more sustainable and encourage consumer activity.  Their goal is to give consumers more knowledge about where their clothes come from and what their impact is on the people and environment involved.  Their main focus is to improve cotton farming methods and increase the use of sustainable cotton practices.  As part of this, they advocate for policy changes to make sustainable farming more accessible to farmers.  One example of policy change that the Textile Exchange has been advocating for is the adoption of the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) to certify organic cotton.  This would be an easy way to meet existing consumer demand for organic cotton and promote environmentally and socially responsible cotton farming.  
  
For a good resource for learning more about cotton, I recommend this interview with one of the Textile Exchange founders.

response:
Of course.  Here's a recipe:


Bourekas (plural: bourekas or bourekhas)
1lb American cheese, grated
1 small bunch fresh chives, chopped
3/4 cup all-purpose flour
3 tbsp all-purpose flour
1 egg
4 tbsp cold chicken-stock (or water)
4-6 medium potatoes, peeled and grated
olive oil

Salt and pepper, to taste


1.  Measure out the flour and pour it onto a plate. Make a well in the center and pour in the egg. Use a fork to break up the yolk. Mix in the grated cheese, and then fold in the remaining ingredients. Turn it into a smooth ball and flatten into a disc.
2.  In a frying pan over medium heat, add a tablespoon of oil, and add one bourekas at a time. When the dough starts to stick to the spoon, turn the bourekas over and fry on the other side.
3.  Once the bourekas have been fried three or four times, get a plate ready and dip into the chicken-stock. Press the bourekas onto the plate and transfer the plate into a warm oven while you finish cooking the others.
4.  Using a deep frying pan over medium-high heat, add a tablespoon of oil. Sauté the grated potato on all sides.
5.  Once the potatoes have been sautéed, drain them and remove them from the pan.
6.  Add the potato to the frying pan with the chicken-stock and allow the potatoes to steam until soft.
7.  Once the potatoes are cooked, turn the bourekas in the chicken stock and allow them to soak up the flavours.
8.  Cut each bourekas into 4 or 8 bite size pieces and place onto a serving platter. Slightly warm one of the potatoes and smear the inside of one and serve with the bourekas.
